pageSubline: Statistical analysis of 3.05M Mexican government procurement contracts

evolution.title: Model Evolution
evolution.subtitle: From expert-weighted checklist (v3.3) to a single supervised ML model with explainability (v5.2 layer).

steps.v33Desc: 8 expert-weighted factors, IMF CRI aligned. AUC barely above random.
steps.v40Desc: Z-score normalization, Bayesian calibration, 9 corruption cases, 12 features.
steps.v50Desc: 12 sector sub-models, 15 labelled cases, temporal train/test split.
steps.v51Desc: 22 cases including SAT EFOS Case 22: 38 RFC-confirmed ghost companies.
steps.v60Desc: ~748 cases, ~603 vendors. Vendor-stratified split (no vendor in both train+test), time-windowed labels, Optuna TPE.
steps.v52Desc: SHAP per-vendor explanations (456K vendors) + PyOD cross-model ensemble (9.3M scores) + KS drift monitoring. See Vendor Profile → Risk tab, Contract detail → AI Confirmed, Dashboard → Cross-Model.
steps.v85Desc: Trained on the case set as of May 2026 (1,401 cases; 1,417 today). One global ElasticNet, 18 active features, c_pu=0.32. HR=11.0%, inside the 2–15% calibration target. Run: CAL-v8-202605020212.

overview.p1End: . The v0.8.5 model was fit on vendor-grouped data. Out of sample, on the 694 vendors added to the case set after training, the model scores AUC 0.656; in sample, across all labelled-case contracts, 0.733 (contract level). The originally reported test AUC of 0.785 could not be reproduced (the training split was not saved) and is no longer cited. A score of 0.35 means this contract's procurement characteristics resemble those of contracts in labelled cases; it is not a probability of corruption.
overview.formulaDescStart: Where z = z-score features, beta = learned coefficients, sigma = logistic sigmoid, c = PU correction (0.32). S(z) is a
overview.formulaDescEnd: — it measures how closely a contract's procurement characteristics resemble those from labelled cases. The score is a pattern-similarity signal, not a corruption probability estimate.
overview.highRiskSummaryEnd: (critical + high). Thresholds were set so the high-risk rate falls inside RUBLI's own 2–15% calibration target. v0.8.5 is the active model (May 2, 2026).
overview.tableFootnote: * 3,051,294 scored contracts of 3,058,286 total. The remaining ~7K contracts lack sector assignment and were excluded from scoring.

features.p1: Each contract is described by 18 z-score features normalized by sector and year baselines. v0.8.5 adds cobid_herfindahl, recency_z, amount_residual_z, amendment_flag, and pub_delay_z to the v5.x behavioral set. The chart below shows the learned ElasticNet coefficients (C=0.2243, l1_ratio=0.7545). Positive coefficients increase the risk score; negative coefficients decrease it.
features.footerNote: Coefficients from Optuna-tuned ElasticNet (C=0.2243, l1_ratio=0.7545, 200 trials). ElasticNet mix balances sparsity and stability. Six features regularized to exactly zero (sameDayContracts, winRate, singleBid, sectorSpread, coBidRate, priceHypConfidence). Run: CAL-v8-202605020212.

riskEvidence.p1: Each risk factor is grounded in peer-reviewed literature on procurement corruption. The table below shows each factor's learned coefficient, global evidence strength, and key source. Hover over a factor name for mechanism details.

findings.finding1Title: Price Volatility is the strongest predictor (+0.558)
findings.finding1Body: Vendors with wildly varying contract sizes carry the largest weight (+0.558), followed by price ratio (+0.358), vendor concentration (+0.327) and co-bid Herfindahl (+0.272). The second-largest coefficient belongs to institution concentration, a Herfindahl index of how much of a vendor's business comes from a single buyer: at −0.388, vendors that sell to one institution score LOWER and vendors spread across many institutions score higher. That runs against the institutional-capture pattern RUBLI describes elsewhere, and it is a known limitation of v0.8.5. Recency (−0.247) measures days since the vendor's previous contract: long gaps lower the score, so frequent repeat contracting raises it.
findings.finding2Title: Key sign changes from v5.1 to v0.8.5
findings.finding2Item1End: — Win rate collapsed from a strong predictor to near-zero. Many GT vendors receive direct awards rather than winning competitive bids, making win_rate a confounded signal.
findings.finding2Item2End: — In v5.1, cross-sector operation was protective. In v0.8.5, large GT vendors like Edenred and Toka operate across sectors, causing the model to associate sector spread with corruption. This is a labeling artifact.
findings.finding2Item3End: — Single bidding provides no discriminating power in v0.8.5. Known-bad vendors tend to win through direct awards rather than single-bid competitive procedures, so this classic OECD indicator has no signal in Mexican federal procurement ground truth.
findings.finding3BodyEnd: — The co_bid_rate coefficient was regularized to exactly 0.0 by L2 regularization. Co-bidding patterns do not help distinguish known-bad contracts from random contracts in this dataset. This suggests the known-bad vendors operate through market concentration rather than collusion.
findings.finding4Strong: These findings challenge the standard OECD/IMF anti-corruption framework
findings.finding4End: for Mexican procurement. The traditional indicators (single bidding, direct awards, short ad periods) that dominate international methodology are weak or reversed in our ground truth data. This may reflect the specific characteristics of Mexican procurement corruption, or the limitations of our ground truth sample.

validation.p1Start: The model was trained on RUBLI's case set:
validation.p1Strong: 1,417 labelled cases (361 from press reports, 25 from official records, 1 audit report, 989 leads the model or ARIA surfaced and analysts wrote up, 41 other)
validation.p1End: . Most cases are analyst write-ups of model-surfaced leads, not adjudicated findings, and unlabelled contracts are treated as negatives even though some are surely corrupt. Case vendors are linked to their contracts within each case window.
validation.footnote: An earlier edition of this page showed a per-case detection table computed with the superseded v5.1 model, which leaked future information into training. It has been withdrawn. Any per-case figures computed with v0.8.5 would be in-sample, because those cases were training positives.
validation.technicalNote: Out of sample, on the 694 vendors added to the case set after training, the model scores AUC 0.656; in sample, across all labelled-case contracts, 0.733 (contract level). The originally reported test AUC of 0.785 could not be reproduced (the training split was not saved) and is no longer cited. Forward holdout: 103,889 contracts of vendors first linked to a case after the May 2 run, against contracts of vendors never in the case set. HR=11.0%, inside RUBLI's own 2–15% calibration target. Run ID: CAL-v8-202605020212.

methods.zScoreP1: Each feature is normalized relative to its sector and year baseline. A direct award in Defensa (where 80% are direct) is less suspicious than in Educacion (where 50% are direct).
methods.zScoreNote: 3,372 baselines computed across 12 sectors, ~24 years, and the 16 original features (the five v2 features are computed separately; 21 in total). Fallback hierarchy: sector+year (if n >= 30), sector-only (if n >= 100), global.
methods.mahalanobisP1: Captures multivariate anomalies — contracts that are unusual across multiple dimensions simultaneously. This replaces the 5 hardcoded interaction pairs from v3.3 with a full covariance-based approach.
methods.mahalanobisNote: Covariance estimated with Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage for stability in small sectors. P-values computed against chi-squared distribution with 16 degrees of freedom.
methods.logisticP1: A single global ElasticNet logistic regression (C=0.2243, l1_ratio=0.7545) trained on contracts of case vendors inside each case window, grouped by vendor. Sector differences enter through the sector-and-year z-score normalization of every feature, not through separate models.
methods.logisticNote: The ElasticNet penalty drives 3 of 21 features (co_bid_rate, price_hyp_confidence, win_rate) to exactly zero. Out of sample, on the 694 vendors added to the case set after training, the model scores AUC 0.656; in sample, across all labelled-case contracts, 0.733 (contract level). The originally reported test AUC of 0.785 could not be reproduced (the training split was not saved) and is no longer cited.
methods.puP1Start: Since unlabeled contracts are not necessarily clean (some may be corrupt but undetected), we apply a Positive-Unlabeled learning correction:
methods.puNote: v0.8.5 uses c = 0.32 (Elkan & Noto). This reflects the heterogeneity of the ground truth. With c=0.32, scores are rescaled by ~3.1x and capped at 1.0. IMPORTANT: The SCAR assumption is structurally violated — known cases are high-profile scandals and model-surfaced leads, not a random sample of all corruption.
methods.bootstrapP1: v0.8.5 does not publish per-contract confidence intervals. Earlier editions of this page described bootstrap intervals; none were computed for this model. Treat small differences between scores as noise.

v52layer.p1End: adds three independent ML tools on top of the active v0.8.5 risk scores. These tools do not replace or alter any contract risk scores — they provide additional explanations and cross-validation signals.
v52layer.shapBody: Shapley values (φᵢ = βᵢ × (zᵢ − E[zᵢ])) computed for each vendor using the global model's coefficients. They cover 16 of the model's 21 features; five newer features (cobid_herfindahl, recency_z, amount_residual_z, amendment_flag, pub_delay_z) are not yet explained, so a vendor's explanation does not sum to its score.
v52layer.shapWhere: Vendor Profile → Risk tab → SHAP Analysis panel
v52layer.pyodBody: Isolation Forest + COPOD ensemble anomaly detection run independently on all 3.05M contracts. A high ensemble score means the contract is a statistical outlier even without knowing the ground truth label.
v52layer.pyodWhere: Contract detail → AI Confirmed badge · Dashboard → Cross-Model Validation · Explore → AI Confirmed filter
v52layer.driftBody: Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests compare the 2024–2025 feature distribution against the 2002–2020 training baseline. Detects when new procurement data develops patterns unlike the training period.
v52layer.aiConfirmedEnd: when the supervised v0.8.5 logistic model scores it as high or critical risk and the unsupervised PyOD ensemble independently scores it above the 0.50 anomaly threshold. Two completely different methods — one trained on labeled corruption cases, one trained on no labels at all — agree that this contract is unusual. This convergence reduces the false-positive rate for investigation triage.
v52layer.noteStart: Note: v5.2 is an analytical overlay — it adds explanability and cross-validation. The active risk model is v0.8.5. Contract
v52layer.noteEnd: values are unchanged by the v5.2 layer.

limitations.item1Text: v0.8.5 was trained on the 1,401 cases that existed on May 2, 2026 (1,417 today), with a per-vendor cap. 989 of today's cases are leads the model or ARIA surfaced and analysts wrote up, so the labels partly reflect the model's own view. Salud and Agricultura contribute a disproportionate share of positive training data due to the IMSS, Segalmex and DICONSA/LICONSA ecosystems.
limitations.item2Text: Cases with few contracts (La Estafa Maestra: 10, Grupo Higa: 3, Oceanografia: 2) have lower detection rates. The model requires sufficient contract volume to detect patterns reliably.
limitations.item3Text: Structure A (2002-2010) has only 0.1% RFC coverage. Z-scores and risk estimates are less reliable for this period. Network analysis requires 2010+ data for meaningful results.
limitations.item4Text: The PU correction (c=0.32) reflects the heterogeneity of expanded GT — many newly added vendors have ambiguous patterns. The SCAR assumption is structurally violated: known cases are high-profile scandals, not a random sample of all corruption.
limitations.item5Text: The co_bid_rate coefficient was regularized to exactly 0.0 in the global model. Co-bidding patterns do not discriminate in our current ground truth.
limitations.item6Text: A high risk score indicates a statistical anomaly consistent with patterns from labelled cases. It does not constitute proof of wrongdoing. Risk scores are intended to prioritize investigation, not determine guilt.

v33section.p1End: with 8 base factors aligned to the IMF Corruption Risk Index methodology. Each factor contributed a percentage of the total score, with interaction bonuses for correlated factor pairs. Scores were preserved in the
v33section.bonusFactors: Additional bonus factors: Co-bidding +5%, Price Hypothesis +5%, Industry Mismatch +3%, Institution Risk +3%. 5 interaction pairs with up to +15% bonus. Score capped at 1.0.

dataSources.p1End: , the Mexican government's official electronic procurement system. The data spans 4 different structures with varying column counts and quality levels.
dataSources.horizonBodyEnd: — the last date the federal government published bulk procurement data. CompraNet, the single comprehensive open-data export this platform is built on, was legally abolished in April 2025 and its bulk feed was frozen on 29 September 2025.
dataSources.horizonNote: Its successor ComprasMX (run by the Secretaría Anticorrupción) has not republished a comprehensive bulk feed. Post-September-2025 contracts now appear only as fragmented, agency-by-agency files (e.g. CFE through January 2026), with most major buyers absent — a real transparency regression. We therefore treat September 2025 as the current data horizon rather than ingest a partial, inconsistent trickle.
dataSources.gapsBody: COMPRANET publishes no annual contracts file for 2004. The register holds only 7 contracts dated that year (7.3 million pesos), against about 54,000 in 2003 and 57,000 in 2005. Treat 2004 as missing data, not a year of low spending, and leave it out of year-over-year comparisons.
dataSources.gapsPartialBody: the federal bulk feed froze on 28 September 2025 after CompraNet was abolished, so 2025 covers about nine months (92,631 contracts, against 143,021 in 2024).
dataSources.datingBody: Each contract is counted in the year of its contract date. Until 30 September 2026, 175,767 contracts published in COMPRANET's 2010 file but signed in 2011 (78,605) or 2012 (97,162), worth 320.6 billion pesos, were counted in 2010. That inflated 2010 and deflated 2011–2012. Because procedure type is only coded from the 2010 file onward, 2011 is the first year with comparable direct-award and single-bid rates. 8,298 recent contracts that carry no contract date keep the year of the file they were published in.
dataSources.rejectEnd: Contracts exceeding 100B MXN are excluded as data entry errors (decimal point mistakes in original COMPRANET data).
dataSources.flagEnd: Contracts between 10B and 100B MXN are included but marked for manual review.
dataSources.context: Context: Mexico's entire federal budget is ~8T MXN annually. A 100B contract would be 1.25% of the national budget.

references.footer: Risk scores are statistical indicators, not verdicts. A high score indicates similarity to patterns in labelled cases -- it does not constitute proof of wrongdoing.

tiers.kicker: HOW TO INTERPRET FINDINGS · CONFIDENCE TIERS
tiers.intro: Not all RUBLI findings carry equal certainty. Every claim — whether in a risk score, an ARIA flag, or a story — belongs to one of three tiers. The tier determines the language you should use when citing or reporting it.
tiers.tierIBody: An independent authority — SAT, SFP, or a documented judicial process — has formally established fraud, simulated operations, or a procurement irregularity.
tiers.tierISource3: · Ground truth cases from official records (25 of 1,417; the rest are press-reported or analyst-labelled)
tiers.tierIIBody: Algorithmic risk signal plus at least one independent external source pointing in the same direction. Neither source alone is conclusive; together they warrant priority investigation.
tiers.tierIIEx1: · Critical risk score + EFOS Presunto match
tiers.tierIIIBodyStart: RUBLI's algorithm detected procurement characteristics that statistically resemble known corruption cases. No external source corroborates the flag.
tiers.tierIIIBodyStrong: Most RUBLI findings are Tier III.
tiers.tierIIISay: "statistical pattern consistent with" · "flagged for investigation" · "behavioral anomaly"
tiers.criticalRuleBody: Never use Tier I language ("confirmed," "proven") for Tier III findings. The RUBLI risk score is not a verdict — it is a triage signal. A score of 0.90 means strong resemblance to patterns from labelled cases, not a 90% probability of guilt. Shell company behavioral pattern flags (P2 pattern) have a 0.7% SAT confirmation rate — the other 99.3% are unconfirmed algorithmic detections.

limitations.intro: These limitations are inherent to the data sources, modeling approach, and legal constraints of the platform. Understanding them is essential to interpreting risk scores correctly.
limitations.interpretationBody: Risk scores are statistical indicators — not verdicts. A high score means strong similarity to patterns from labelled cases. A low score does not certify a contract is clean. Use scores for investigation triage only; follow-up with primary sources to establish facts.
